newsitem.title: USA: IBM reorganizes sales and services units.
newsitem.headline: IBM reorganizes sales and services units.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp said that it is reorganizing its global sales and services businesses, and as part of that focus, it will operate services under a single brand, IBM Global Services.
IBM said its global services organization has been operating in some countries outside the U.S. under a lot of different names, and this move should clarify the IBM brand.
An IBM spokesman said that the moves were made to make its organization operate more effectively.
The Armonk, N.Y.-based computer giant also named Lucio Stanca, general manager, global marketing operations.

Stanca, who has headed IBM's Europe, Middle East, Africa (EMEA) since the fall of 1994, will continue as chairman of EMEA, based in Paris. Stanca will be heading up a new single direct marketing focus throughout the world by IBM, which will now have a single operational focus.

Previously, IBM's direct marketing efforts have been in various geographies, without a single consistent focus. Direct marketing refers to direct mail, telemarketing and electronic marketing via the Internet, in 159 countries.
Succeeding Stanca as EMEA general manager is William Etherington, who was general manager of IBM Industries.
IBM's Industries unit is the business which manages 11 industry-specific business units.

The industry specific units will now be managed on a global basis by David Thomas, who was general manager, IBM North America. In his new role, as general manager, Global Industries, Thomas will be responsible for IBM's industry specific strategies, performance and solutions portfolio.

He will be succeeded in North America by John Thompson, who had been general manager of IBM's personal software products, which has responsibility for IBM's beleaguered operating system, OS/2. No replacement was named.

An IBM spokesman said that a replacement will be named for Thompson, and that the move was just another one of the "dominos falling" in a big executive reorganization and that IBM will name a replacement for Thompson in personal software.
"Some people are saying, what does this mean for OS/2?" said the IBM spokesman. "It means no change whatsoever in strategy...We have not selected anyone yet."

While IBM's OS/2 software has made significant inroads, by its count of about 13 million users now, it is still a paltry share of the world personal computer market, dominated by Microsoft Corp's Windows operating system.

At Internet World this week, IBM chairman and CEO told reporters in brief comments at the IBM booth that IBM remains committed to OS/2. "Absolutely, in a networked world," he said when asked if IBM was still committed to OS/2.
IBM issued its organization changes in an internal memo.

"In the last three years, we have aggressively adapted our business to meet the changing requirements of our customers around the world," said Ned Lautenbach, senior vice president, and group executive, sales and services, in the memo. "Customer requirements dictate that we operate globally."
